Northern snake-necked turtles (Chelodina oblonga) hatch from leathery-shelled eggs after an extended incubation period. When eggs are held at a constant temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], emergence from the nest occurs at approximately 200 days [ab = approximately 200 days], a developmental duration that is comparatively long among Australasian chelids. Newly emerged neonates typically exhibit a plastron length at birth of 3.1 cm [Lb = 3.1 cm] and possess a wet weight at birth of 14.3 grams [Wwb = 14.3 grams]; this initial mass reflects the substantial yolk reserves packed into the parchment-shelled eggs, which measure roughly 35 millimeters in length and 28 millimeters in width. The slow pace of embryonic development at this thermal regime likely imposes a constraint on recruitment in seasonal wetlands, as hatchlings emerging late in the austral summer must locate suitable aquatic refuges before ephemeral water bodies contract.

Sexual maturation in this long-lived chelid proceeds along divergent trajectories for males and females, a pattern common among turtles with pronounced sexual size dimorphism. At a rearing temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], male individuals attain puberty after approximately 3.9 years since birth [tp = approximately 3.9 years since birth], at which point their plastron length is around 16.5 centimeters [Lp = around 16.5 centimeters]. Females, by contrast, require a longer period to reach reproductive maturity, with puberty occurring roughly 6.5 years after birth [tp = roughly 6.5 years after birth] when the plastron measures about 21.0 centimeters [Lp = about 21.0 centimeters] at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This nearly two-fold difference in pubertal timing corresponds to the greater body size threshold females must achieve before gonadal activation commences, a life-history adaptation that prioritizes accumulation of structural mass for future egg production.

Adult body size, particularly the maximum plastron length attained by females, represents a key determinant of lifetime reproductive output in C. oblonga. The ultimate plastron length for females reaches approximately 30.0 centimeters [Li = approximately 30.0 centimeters], while males achieve a smaller asymptotic size, with their ultimate plastron length recorded at about 25.0 centimeters [Li = about 25.0 centimeters]. This sexual size dimorphism is among the most pronounced observed within the genus Chelodina and is likely driven by fecundity selection, as larger females can accommodate greater clutch volumes. The substantial difference in adult body size also influences foraging ecology and habitat use, with adult females capable of exploiting larger prey items, such as crustaceans and fish, that remain inaccessible to smaller conspecifics, thereby reducing intraspecific competition.

Reproductive output in Chelodina oblonga is tightly linked to female body size, particularly once individuals exceed the pubertal size threshold. Field studies indicate that a sexually mature female with a plastron length of 29 centimeters produces approximately 14 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 14 eggs per clutch] in a single annual nesting event [F_R_i = single annual nesting event], a rate observed under the thermal conditions typical of the species' southern range, where average water temperatures hover near 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This reproductive strategy concentrates offspring emergence when aquatic habitat is most extensive and prey availability for yolk-sac larvae is at its peak.

Maximum longevity in the northern snake-necked turtle remains incompletely characterized, though available records provide an estimate. Captive individuals at a stable temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] have been documented to survive for up to 14.1 years [am = up to 14.1 years], although this lifespan estimate is tentative given the paucity of long-term mark-recapture studies in wild populations. Field-based observations suggest that wild individuals may live considerably longer, as chelonians typically exhibit extended lifespans in natural settings compared to captive conditions. Future research employing stable isotope analysis or long-term telemetry could refine this estimate, which is critical for understanding the population dynamics of this species, particularly given its delayed maturation and low annual reproductive output relative to other freshwater turtles. Such demographic parameters render C. oblonga especially vulnerable to chronic disturbance.
